entries.title: Johnson’s Political Future May Hinge on Republicans Exceeding Midterm Expectations
entries.summary: The speaker says he hasn’t entertained the idea of serving as minority leader, insisting Republicans will win. But if they lose the majority GOP lawmakers expect someone else to get the post.
entries.content:
BETHLEHEM, Pa. — Speaker Mike Johnson is in the middle of a 30-day campaign stretch stumping for vulnerable Republican members and top challengers who will decide the majority come November. But Johnson’s political fate is likely tied to theirs.

The midterms will effectively decide if President Donald Trump’s lame-duck era starts in 2027 or if he has two more years of Republican control in Congress to move his agenda. If Democrats retake the gavel, the job description of the top Republican leader will change dramatically and the House GOP conference may look elsewhere for a figure to push back against a slew of investigations of the Trump administration.

Prior to a campaign stop for Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pennsylvania), Johnson dismissed the idea he would need to entertain a run for minority leader.

“We're going to win, so I don't have to answer that question,” Johnson told NOTUS in an interview at Saucon Valley Country Club. “I intend to be the speaker going forward.”

Johnson claims to have the hardest job “in the world” navigating a two-seat majority with colleagues who routinely curse at him, call him names and refuse to be team players. But, through it all he continues to want to lead the conference, even with the constant backlash that comes with it.

Sometimes that blowback comes from Trump, who has at times joked that he has two jobs: being president and being speaker, due to the fact he is often the closer to secure the votes for Republican priority bills.

But the speaker says others in the White House view it differently.

“Some on his staff have said, ‘No, it's really like you’re co-president,’” Johnson recalled to NOTUS. “Because the president and I speak all the time.”

But the harshest criticisms of Johnson at times come from his own members. Some have stormed out of rooms and slammed doors on him, blocked key priority bills or just refused to vote with leadership altogether.

Still, Johnson says he doesn’t take it personally.

“I don't get my feelings hurt. I never do,” Johnson said. “With leadership comes attacks and, you know, defamatory remarks and all. That's just part of the job. You're going to be criticized no matter what you do.”

He also claims he doesn’t hold any grudges against the members who launch personal attacks.

Referring to a Bible verse, Johnson said he wants to practice “the ministry of reconciliation” and always be open “to bring people back into the fold.”

“I don’t do this job for the praise of men. I do it because it’s a responsibility,” he said.

Despite this approach, it doesn’t mean he’s totally opposed to punishing members who aren’t team players.

Johnson said there have been close to “100 members who have come forward with ideas” on how to adjust the conference rules to reprimand members who derail Republican legislation.

“That's the cart before the horse,” he added. “I mean, when we are organizing for the next Congress, I suspect there will be some proposed amendments to the rules to try to adjust that.”

Johnson has led the Republican conference through three successful — while at times tumultuous — years. He gets credit for uniting the various factions to pass Trump’s signature tax bill in 2025. But now comes his biggest test: the midterms.

Similar to Johnson, a lot of top leaders spend their August traveling across the country to campaign for top-tier candidates.

In August, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise visited 13 states and 19 cities to campaign with 18 members and 12 GOP challengers. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer has made stops in Ohio and Pennsylvanie while recovering from foot surgery. House Ways and Means Chair Jason Smith has been to seven states to campaign with 11 candidates, and House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan has so far been to seven states and campaigned with 10 candidates.

But Johnson has a lot more riding on the midterms than others.

If the Republicans are to pull it out and keep the majority, his position atop the Republican conference is all but secure. But if they lose the majority, Johnson’s future becomes much more uncertain.

Republicans across the House GOP conference, including some in leadership, don’t believe Johnson will run for minority leader and will step down from House leadership.

The speaker insisted to NOTUS he isn’t imagining life in the minority. “Really, I never thought about it,” he said.

But others in the conference are thinking about it.

NOTUS has previously reported on Jordan’s apparent angling for a leadership position. Scalise and Emmer are also viewed as contenders for the top spot should Republicans lose the majority.

Still, if Republicans lose in November, there will be a fight for the top spots.

“In the political burn down that’s coming, we slaughter everybody at the front of the room,” one senior GOP member told NOTUS.

entries.title: Who Will Survive the Commanders’ Cuts? Projecting the 53-Man Roster.
entries.summary: With one preseason game remaining, Washington has some tough decisions to make.
entries.content:
Two preseason games are in the can and the Commanders’ final roster cutdowns are less than a week away on Sunday.

Most of the team’s starters are set in stone, but there are almost 30 other spots on the roster up for grabs. Here is a projection of what Washington’s final roster may look like.

(The number in parentheses is how many players Washington kept at the position last season.)

QUARTERBACK (3)

  • Jayden Daniels
  • Marcus Mariota
  • Athan Kaliakmanis
If Mariota hadn’t sprained the MCL in his right knee during the first preseason game, the Commanders may have elected to keep just two quarterbacks. But with the uncertainty of Mariota’s return, Kaliakmanis gets the nod. The rookie has taken more third-team reps than Sam Hartman in practice since last week, which may signal his position in the pecking order.

RUNNING BACK (4)

  • Bill Croskey-Merritt
  • Rachaad White
  • Kaytron Allen
  • Jeremy McNichols
McNichols sustained a quad injury that will keep him out for a few weeks. In his absence, undrafted rookie Robert Henry Jr. grabbed the brass ring against the Dolphins two weeks ago (12 rushes for 75 yards), but followed that up by running for negative-3 yards and fumbling a kick return against the Lions. The rookie may have had the nod for the fourth spot at one point, but McNichols is more dependable.

RECEIVER (5)

  • Terry McLaurin
  • Stefon Diggs
  • Antonio Williams
  • Dyami Brown
  • Jaylin Lane
  • Luke McCaffrey
It’s ironic that the receivers group is the most difficult unit to pare down. This was an area of weakness when practices started back in June. But the arrival of Diggs on Aug. 7 has created a bit of a roster crunch. McLaurin, Diggs and the rookie Williams are safe. Lane and McCaffrey double as the team’s punt and kick returner, respectively, which earns them each a spot. If it comes down to Brown and Treylon Burks, I’d give Brown the nod because he seems to have more of a connection with Daniels during practice — not to mention that Burks has had difficulty staying healthy over his five-year career.

TIGHT END (4)

  • Chig Okonkwo
  • John Bates
  • Ben Sinnott
  • Colson Yankoff
Okonkwo, Bates and Sinnott are all easy locks. Yankoff, an undrafted free agent in 2024, has had the second-most-impressive camp among the tight ends behind Okonkwo. Commanders quarterbacks could throw a pass into the bleachers and Yankoff would probably come down with it — he’s made jumping, diving and sliding catches all over the field. With the uncertainty surrounding the rest of the offensive line, there will probably be a lot of two-tight-end sets this season, making this group an important cog in the offense.

OFFENSIVE LINE (9)

  • Brandon Coleman
  • Chris Paul
  • Max Scharping
  • Nick Allegretti
  • Julian Good-Jones
  • Matt Gulbin
  • Sam Cosmi
  • Andrew Wylie
  • Josh Conerly Jr.
The offensive line came into camp as a strength for Washington, but it fell apart immediately. Allegretti (calf) didn’t practice from July 30 to Aug. 17 and missed two more practices — and the Lions game — late last week. Pro Bowl left tackle Laremy Tunsil tore his triceps on Aug. 8 and probably won’t return before the end of the season. Wylie gets the nod here because Trent Scott has struggled in the preseason: On Saturday, he gave up a sack and allowed his defender to blow up a rush. With Allegretti’s health up in the air, the Commanders are likely to keep three centers.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

DEFENSIVE LINE (8)

  • Tim Settle
  • Shy Tuttle
  • Daron Payne
  • Javon Kinlaw
  • Charles Omenihu
  • Ricky Barber
This unit is pretty beat up. Veteran Deatrich Wise Jr. hasn’t practiced since tearing his right quad nearly a year ago, and Jer’Zhan Newton will, according to coach Dan Quinn, miss a "significant amount of time" after having surgery to repair a pec that he tore last week. Settle and Payne have missed time as well. Barber has been a bright spot all preseason and narrowly beats out veteran Byron Cowart for the final spot.

LINEBACKER (7)

  • Odafe Oweh
  • Joshua Josephs
  • Frankie Luvu
  • Sonny Styles
  • Leo Chenal
  • K’Lavon Chaisson
  • Dorance Armstrong
  • Javontae Jean-Baptiste
With the switch to a 3-4 alignment under defensive coordinator Daronte Jones, I foresee the Commanders keeping some extra players. Josephs, the rookie out of Tennessee, has had one of the most surprising camps of anyone, both as a pass rusher and run stopper. Jean-Baptiste has come on late and has probably earned a spot on the outside.

CORNERBACK (5)

  • Trey Amos
  • Rasul Douglas
  • Amik Robertson
  • Mike Sainristil
  • Antonio Hamilton Sr.
It’s unclear when Amos will return after injuring his ankle Aug. 8. It’s the same leg in which he broke his fibula last season, so the team is taking a cautious approach in bringing him back. If Amos can’t go right away, Douglas will probably start across from Robertson, with Sainristil in the nickel. Hamilton, an 11-year veteran, has done just enough in coverage and special teams to stave off fourth-year vet Darius Rush and undrafted rookie Fred Davis II.

SAFETY (5)

  • Nick Cross
  • Jeremy Reaves
  • Tyler Owens
  • Percy Butler
  • Quan Martin
Cross and Reaves have almost exclusively run with the first-team defense during training camp. Former starter Will Harris, 30, has been in the mix as well, but Owens, Butler and Martin (another former starter) all play special teams and are under the age of 27. Owens, a hybrid linebacker, blew up a Lions running back in pass protection on Saturday, the kind of highlight play that probably bumps him up the roster.

SPECIAL TEAMS (3)

  • Punter Tress Way
  • Kicker Drew Stevens
  • Long snapper Tyler Ott
Stevens locked in his spot last week when the Commanders cut Jake Moody. The rookie out of Iowa has been impressive all camp, hitting kicks as far as 60 yards. The true test will come in the regular season when the game might come down to Stevens’ leg, but for the time being the Commanders seem to have found an answer at kicker.

entries.title: Three Convicted Political Scammers Want Trump’s Pardon Mercy
entries.summary: Richard Zeitlin, William Tierney and Matt Tunstall went to prison for scamming tens of thousands of Americans — including many MAGA acolytes.
entries.content:
A rise in presidential pardons for white-collar criminals has given hope to fraudsters of a different flavor.

Three convicted political scammers — Richard Zeitlin, William Tierney and Matt Tunstall — have formally sought pardons from President Donald Trump, seeking the same leniency the president has shown a number of felonious cryptocurrency, finance and health care executives.

Zeitlin, Tierney and Tunstall collectively swindled tens of thousands of Americans, including Trump supporters, of over $120 million, according to court records. Their individual schemes involved the creation, operation or support of fraudulent political committees, charitable organizations and robocall operations that employed dishonest fundraising tactics, such as adopting false identities and even impersonating Trump.

The trio’s requests injected new intrigue into what’s become a pardon-system free-for-all.

Since Trump granted clemency to nearly 1,600 Jan. 6 riot defendants just after taking office in 2025, pardons have become less of a methodical, Justice Department-administered process and more of a psyop. A pay-to-pardon environment emerged, with wealthy criminals offering wads of cash to lobbyists claiming MAGA connections — attracting a diverse criminal clientele, from rappers and CEOs to crypto bros.

“If you’re a scammer of any kind — a white-collar criminal, generally — you’re going to be made hopeful by all this,” Frank Bowman, professor emeritus at the University of Missouri School of Law who is publishing a book on the history of pardons, told NOTUS. “They’re going to certainly think of themselves as being analogous to a lot of the folks who’ve gotten sort of Trumpian largesse.”

The Trump administration last month denied Tunstall’s request, and the White House team that reviews clemency requests is not currently tracking those of Zeitlin and Tierney, according to a White House official. The official described the review process as “thorough,” with Trump delivering the final verdict.

“President Trump has exercised his constitutional authority to issue pardons and commutations for a variety of individuals,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement to NOTUS. Bis criticized how President Joe Biden and Democratic governors used their pardon power, saying Biden pardoned and commuted the sentences of dangerous individuals and people in the country illegally.

Representatives for Zeitlin, Tierney and Tunstall couldn’t be reached for comment.

After building a telemarketing empire that for decades took advantage of unsuspecting donors, Zeitlin was convicted of a litany of offenses in 2023, including wire fraud. Zeitlin’s telemarketing business raised money for political action committees that purported to support an array of causes — many associated with conservatives — including police safety, military veterans and children with cancer. But authorities said he kept most of that money for himself.
Richard.Zeitlin (895x852, AR: 1.05)Zeitlin received a 10-year prison sentence in 2024. This year, he filed paperwork with the Justice Department to have his sentence commuted. His request is pending.

Tierney operated six scam PACs and defrauded tens of thousands of small-dollar donors through calls and mailed solicitations, according to the U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of New York. The groups claimed to support causes including law enforcement and the anti-abortion movement.

Tierney used multiple fake identities to perpetuate the charade. Less than 1% of the money raised supported the advertised causes. Tierney pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and in 2019 was sentenced to two years in prison and over $1 million in restitution. He has hired the Vogel Group, a D.C.-based lobbying and consulting firm, for $100,000, according to lobbying disclosures. His pardon request is also pending.

While Zeitlin and Tierney probably defrauded tens of thousands of Trump supporters, Tunstall literally impersonated the president.

Using robocalls impersonating Trump and his campaign, Tunstall raised over $3.4 million by 2021, according to CNN. He spent most of the money on more robocalls, but funneled at least $738,000 to himself. A federal judge sentenced him to 10 years in prison in 2023. Tunstall applied for Trump to commute his sentence last year.

Tunstall’s use of Trump’s name for personal enrichment could explain why his request was denied on July 10, among a batch of denials that focused on clearing a backlog of older pardon requests.

“If you’ve got some guy who’s directly going out and impersonating Trump personally, but not cutting Trump in,” Bowman said, “that seems to me to be a low-probability application for success.”

Perhaps the closest analogue to Zeitlin’s and Tierney’s cases was Michele Fiore. Fiore was convicted in 2024 after she raised $70,000 for a memorial honoring slain Las Vegas police officer Alyn Beck. She spent the money on rent, a wedding and plastic surgery.

Trump pardoned Fiore, a former Nevada state lawmaker and Las Vegas City Council member, in April of last year before she was sentenced. But Fiore’s case differed in a significant way: She is an ardent Trump supporter.

Support or past affiliation with Trump has been a recurring characteristic of pardon recipients during his second term. Zeitlin and Tierney lack strong MAGA credentials.

“Because specifically it’s Trump that they’re leveraging through their frauds to make money, that’s going to make it less probable that they’re going to get granted clemency,” said Mark Osler, a pardon expert and law professor at the University of St. Thomas. “Right now, you have a lot of people who are petitioning for clemency who aren’t getting it — you know, who don’t have that baggage.”

Presidents have historically wielded the pardon power in a different way than Trump. For example, advisers from the Justice Department’s pardon office typically recommended for presidential consideration applicants who showed remorse and had served their sentence.

Trump began unraveling these norms during his first term. President Joe Biden also made ethicists cringe, issuing pardons to his son, Hunter, and others, such as former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Director Anthony Fauci, that detractors considered politically motivated. Trump’s immediate pardon of the Jan. 6 defendants made political pardons the status quo, deprioritizing the office tasked with examining applicants.

“When I was pardon attorney, political support was not something that we took into consideration in any way, shape or form,” Elizabeth Oyer, who served in that role from 2022 to March 2025, told NOTUS. “The pardon process is intended to be nonpolitical.”

Attorney General Todd Blanche fired Oyer after she refused to recommend that actor and director Mel Gibson, a prominent Trump supporter, have his gun rights restored, according to Oyer. The U.S. pardon attorney role is not a political appointment.

“There are thousands of people who have applied through the ordinary Justice Department process, who do not have political connections or money to spend on lobbyists,” Oyer said. “Those people are being overlooked in favor of the wealthy and well-connected.”

“That is fundamentally at odds with how the pardon process is supposed to work,” she added.

Tunstall and Zeitlin weren’t only seeking presidential pardons to win their freedom.

In February, Tunstall requested a compassionate release from prison. He cited his father-in-law’s failing health and inability to properly care for Tunstall’s daughter. “I pose no threat to the community as I have demonstrated excellent behavior not only rehabilitating myself, but also helping others,” Tunstall wrote to a federal judge, adding that he would be a “loving father and productive member of society” if released.
Tunstall (1344x852, AR: 1.58)The judge denied Tunstall’s request three days after receiving it.

Tunstall, who is imprisoned in Mendota, California, is expected to remain incarcerated until December 2030.

Zeitlin is imprisoned at a federal penitentiary in Montgomery, Alabama. In March, he sued the prison warden, arguing he should be eligible to be released a month earlier than scheduled. If Zeitlin’s lawsuit is successful, he would be eligible for prerelease custody on Aug. 1, 2031, according to the warden’s response to the lawsuit.

Tierney completed his sentence in 2021.

It’s unclear whether efforts by Zeitlin and Tierney will ever win Trump’s attention and favor. Then again, Trump has issued a number of unexpected pardons during the past 20 months.

“One thing that we know is that presidents tend to favor, with clemency, the kind of people they have empathy for,” Osler said. “Where they can see a little bit of themselves in that person.”

entries.title: The Kids Competing to Make America Patriotic Again
entries.summary: In the heartland, debates were set aside and everyone — for a moment — was on the same team.
entries.content:
HARPERSFIELD TOWNSHIP, Ohio – The White House had chosen one boy to lead a reading from the Bible, so Reagan Tuck Dukes III, the blond-haired, blue-eyed linebacker from Texas, stood before dozens of other teens who had come from all across the country for a new athletic contest known as the Patriot Games.

They’d all heard the haters online who called it propaganda, compared it to the Hunger Games, blasted its overwhelming whiteness and labeled its athletes the new Hitler Youth. But none of that fazed RT. He’d just come back from a weeklong mission trip to Peru and understood how lucky he was to live in the United States of America.

The room was full of his people. They loved Jesus and sports and the flag. The night before, they’d marveled at the stories of a Medal of Honor recipient who’d saved lives in Vietnam. And they’d heard his message: “Remember: Everyone is Team USA.” But RT knew they all felt tempted to chase personal glory. Everyone wanted one of the two $125,000 scholarships; everyone wanted to be crowned champion by the president. So, RT chose Hebrews 12:1-2.

“Since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off everything that hinders and the sin that so easily entangles,” he said. “And let us run with perseverance the race marked out for us.”

It was mid-August, the waning days of summer, the twilight of the nation’s 250th anniversary celebrations. The party planners at Freedom 250 had pulled off a series of hurried, expensive spectacles, including a prayer rally, a state fair and a mixed-martial-arts bout on the lawn of the White House. And even though their national civics competition was marred by accusations of bias, they had also set a record for the biggest fireworks display of all time.

The Patriot Games were in part an attempt to reach Gen Z, which polling shows is far less patriotic than older generations in a country where overall national pride just hit a 25-year low. In a June Gallup poll, only 14% of adults under 34 said they were “extremely proud” to be an American.
20260812_McGarvey_PatriotGames_4458 copy.jpg (4926x3284, AR: 1.50)20260812_McGarvey_PatriotGames_4609 copy.jpg (4551x3034, AR: 1.50)20260812_McGarvey_PatriotGames_0425 copy.jpg (8026x5350, AR: 1.50)A few kids were trying to do their part. The girl representing the Cherokee Nation had said in her application that she wanted to help bring patriotism back to the U.S. The boy from Mississippi said he would’ve been here even if the commander-in-chief was Joe Biden. And RT understood that he’d been selected because he’d attracted an audience on social media by posting faith-based videos, such as when he walked through a field carrying a barbell with “the weight Jesus did on the cross.”

“No matter where you fall in this competition, your race isn’t over,” RT said.

Not long after, the kids tied on bandanas, Sharpied Bible verses onto their skin and underlined their eyes with stripes of red, white and blue. They took the field as MAGA hats filled the stands, the national anthem blared from the speakers and a 200-person crew from ESPN turned on its cameras. The hosts welcomed America to a youth sports academy called SPIRE in a speck of pastoral heartland.

Outside these walls, Harpersfield was a small town grappling with the challenges of modern rural life. But it had dropped everything to assume the role of Everytown, USA. The people shared a mindset: We’re going to roll up our sleeves, be together, smile. And it was here, under the hot lights of TV, that President Donald Trump’s vision for the country reached full, ephemeral bloom.

* * *

Down on the turf, waiting for field day to start, one girl turned to her group.

“We’re, like, all blond!” she said.

The girl from Washington state, one of the few brunettes, quickly chimed in.

“I was blond when I was a baby.”

Who were these kids? The selection process was rigorous, organizers say. The kids had to answer prompts, disclose their sex assigned at birth and list places outside their home state where they had a “meaningful personal, family, cultural, military, or community connection.” Freedom 250 and a youth sports company called 3STEP picked 60 boys and 60 girls based on their essay, video and athleticism.

In the stands, parents described a murky, chaotic process. Applications had opened just six weeks ago, and they learned their kids were selected about a week before kickoff. They got no information on which sports would be included.

One man suggested the administration didn’t promote it well “to keep out advocacy for certain issues.” The grandmother of the girl representing Guam speculated that Big Tech had suppressed ads because of the event’s ties to Trump.

“I’m a big conspiracy theorist,” she said.

When the kids learned they were in, they freaked out. They flooded social media with AI graphics, reaction videos and unboxings of a welcome package that included a commemorative coin featuring Trump's as-yet-unrealized 250-foot arch.
Patriot Games 2026By the time they took the field, at least seven kids were representing places they did not live. The girl representing Maine was from New Hampshire; the New Jersey boy went to school in Texas. One boy jokingly cheered on his friend representing Puerto Rico by yelling, “Let’s go Alabama-Virginia-Washington, D.C.!”

Field day included six stations: broad jump, flexed-arm hang, “pro agility shuttle,” 100-meter dash, 55-meter hurdles and an event no one had ever seen in which kids threw medicine balls as far as they could.

Unlike the civics contest, the Patriot Games had transparent scoring. The kids got 60 points for winning an individual event, 59 for finishing second and so on. Organizers wanted even teams for dodgeball and kickball, so they paired the highest- and lowest-ranked players. The ESPN livestream, which was playing on a couple of big TVs, occasionally flashed an update.

Even as the scoreboard separated them, it was hard not to see the kids as winners already winning. They had founded clubs and won elections. They built robots and spoke multiple languages. One girl with cerebral palsy played lacrosse and advocated for the disabled. Many had well-connected parents. There was the son of the athletic director at the University of Georgia. The grandson of a tech entrepreneur. The younger sister of the girl who’d won the national civics contest, whose father led Wyoming Catholic College and was a close friend of the president of the conservative Heritage Foundation. Other parents kept walking up to shake hands with RT Dukes II, a prominent oil-and-gas executive who last year received a cash bonus of $135,000.

Dukes’ son was something of a celebrity. Freedom 250 collaborated with him on social media; the public relations staff highlighted him as often as it could; and when he caught a line drive in kickball, someone else’s dad yelled, “Let’s go, Texas!”

In the background, monitoring it all, was SPIRE CEO Jonathan Ehrenfeld. The Baltimore-based real estate investor said he had purchased the northern Ohio sports academy in 2019 because he believed the U.S. was ready for another elite academy like IMG in Florida. It was also a good deal; he paid $7.4 million for a campus that had cost $100 million to build. Ehrenfeld then built hotels and restaurants, expanded its facilities and purchased farms for future development. A local columnist mourned the pivot from community to profit.

It's not clear why Freedom 250 put the games in Ohio instead of D.C., as was originally announced. Ehrenfeld is not a big political donor and said Freedom 250 approached him in early summer. Together, he said, they pulled off a two-year event in two months. He declined to disclose the terms of their deal; Freedom 250 declined to say how much the event cost and how much of that cost was covered by taxpayers.
20260812_McGarvey_PatriotGames_1825 copy.jpg (7850x5233, AR: 1.50)20260812_McGarvey_PatriotGames_1881 copy.jpg (7709x5139, AR: 1.50)20260812_McGarvey_PatriotGames_0118 copy 2.jpg (8039x5360, AR: 1.50)As the kids left the field for the day, two people were still out there working. Jim and Jimmy Doherty, the longtime father-and-son garbagemen of Harpersfield, had heard the Secret Service needed 30, 8-foot-tall steel dumpsters ASAP. It was Jimmy’s only day off; he was supposed to take his young son fishing. But instead, he spent eight hours blocking off a stretch of tree line because it could, a couple nights later, offer a gunman a good shot at the president.

Inside, the kids were relaxing, recovering, dancing, gaming, flirting, posting, bonding and staying up past curfew. Outside, Jim and Jimmy were finishing what some had started referring to as “the border wall.” They didn’t know who would pay them or when. But it was a job that needed doing — and they, like the kids, were proud to have been called.

* * *

The next morning, Marie Paul leaned on a railing overlooking a turf field. Her daughter Oluwasheyi, who had just run a course of mashed-up sports known as the “varsity circuit,” was napping. Paul still couldn’t believe they were here.

Shay, as her daughter was known, hadn’t applied until about a week ago. She was a gymnast and sprinter who didn’t play traditional team sports. But a week earlier, Paul had gotten a text from an acquaintance who said there’d been a last-minute injury, and did Shay want to represent her home in the U.S. Virgin Islands?

Paul had hesitated. She believed the event was another Republican political tool. She suspected they’d be some of the only Black people there. But she had always been an independent thinker, and to her, the calculus was simple.

You have an agenda? Well, so do I.

Paul wanted Shay to see the world. Meet people. Be on ESPN. Learn from other athletes. Feel deep soreness in her arms and find within herself the will to keep fighting.
MariePaul_Shay.jpg (2438x1500, AR: 1.63)The night before, Shay had come home upset. A boy had high-fived all his teammates except her. Paul knew it wasn’t a white-Black thing — the boy was also Black. Maybe he skipped Shay on purpose, maybe Shay misread the situation. Either way, Paul didn’t want her daughter’s discomfort to linger, so she talked to the coaches, who brought the kids together. The boy apologized and said he meant it as a joke.

“She felt better about it,” Paul said, and just that one small lesson in communication made the whole trip worth it.

As Paul kept telling me stories, a PR official came over to the empty bleachers and stood behind her. Paul hesitated, then continued, saying that she appreciated Freedom 250 including far-flung territories in the event.

“Because it is difficult to be patriotic when you are —”

“Sorrrryyyy,” the official interrupted. She explained there was a new media policy: The handful of independent reporters at the event could stand only in certain areas, and if they wanted to move, they had to be accompanied by a PR official, who would also approve and observe all interviews.

Later, it would become clear that Freedom 250 had created the policy in response to a story in The Washington Post. One anonymous ESPN staffer had suggested that the government bullied the Walt Disney Company, which owns ESPN, into televising the event as part of a broader fight that had already ensnared comedian Jimmy Kimmel and some of the company’s broadcast licenses.

The PR official allowed me to ask a few final questions. Paul said she empathized with the government’s struggle to control the narrative taught to children in the age of social media. And she praised the Patriot Games as a rare and invaluable cultural exchange for the Virgin Islands.

“My daughter feels more included within her country than ever before,” she said.

I asked Paul if we could sit together to watch Shay’s next event.

Yes, she said.

No, the PR official said.

The official shepherded me back to the media viewing area.

* * *

On the other end of the facility, a boy named Christian Berezay was crawling, high-stepping and weaving through a military-style obstacle course called “Operation Endurance.”

“Let’s go, Christian!” D.J. Berezay hollered, trying to fulfill his son’s request to be the loudest parent in the building.

In the past year, D.J. said, he had witnessed a miracle. His son, who is on the autism spectrum, had always struggled to focus. But then his mom heard about a medication called leucovorin. Typically prescribed to moderate harmful effects of cancer drugs, it was now being touted by the Trump administration as a treatment for autism. Nationwide prescriptions surged 700%.

In March, the Food and Drug Administration said there wasn’t enough evidence to approve leucovorin as a treatment for autism. But the Berezays were already believers. Christian said the pill made his brain wake up, and in months, his parents said, his reading level jumped from first grade to ninth. He started winning wrestling matches.

D.J. knew there were better athletes than his son in the state of Washington, but even if they’d applied, he figured Christian was chosen in part to highlight an underdog’s story.

Down on the course, Christian somersaulted over an A-frame, tip-toed across an L-shaped balance beam, flipped a big tire, caught it before it hit the ground and flipped it again, which made a couple parents ooh.

“I have to thank the Holy Father for giving me this opportunity,” Christian told ESPN.
20260812_McGarvey_PatriotGames_3527 copy.jpg (7951x5303, AR: 1.50)All afternoon, the kids cheered each other on. They celebrated excellence but were loudest when group-mates labored through monkey bars or whiffed at T-ball or struggled to serve a volleyball over the net. The final stage of the “varsity circuit” was running the bases, and even though several kids missed home plate, no one made them go back and touch it.

“It’s not a normal athletic event,” a security guard told a volunteer. “They all want each other to win.”

Early in the evening, the coaches gathered the kids to announce the Top 16. RT made it as the boy’s No. 12 seed; Christian and Shay did not advance. The semifinals started right away. They split into groups for tug-of-war and played several rounds of head-to-head Pop-A-Shot. In both games, the winners each got 30 points. The kids were tracking the scores now, and when the boy from Florida beat RT in Pop-A-Shot, he jumped up and down, because he knew he’d secured the last spot in the finals.

As a coach announced the final four, RT stood in place, his mouth a thin line. But when the girls screamed and mobbed each other, and the crowd started chanting "USA!," he smiled and dapped everyone up. It was just as the Medal of Honor recipient had said: Everyone was on the same team.

* * *

The morning the president would arrive, Deputy John Jacobson from the county sheriff’s office got a request to check out a white cargo van parked across the street from SPIRE. He detained the driver, a New York City resident from Ukraine who did not speak English, and called the bomb squad. The dog sniffed and went nuts. Jacobson shut down nearby businesses and roadways.

Officers interviewed the driver with a translator app and reviewed receipts. It turned out there was no threat; the driver was just delivering confetti cannons to the Patriot Games.

The incident captured how hard the community was straining to look its best in front of the nation. While Trump had campaigned at SPIRE in 2016, the local paper reported that no sitting president had visited Ashtabula County since Abraham Lincoln. And the county was ecstatic to host this president — after voting for Reagan twice, then Democrats seven straight times, it flipped to Trump in 2016 and ran up the score for him in 2020 and 2024, when he won by nearly 30 points.

To prepare, Ehrenfeld had asked the trustees to pretty up Harpersfield. The trustees could be wary of Ehrenfeld’s grand plans, which had brought a surge in traffic and contributed to a drop in water pressure as the little community swelled. But they saw the Games as an honor and an opportunity. In addition to hosting the president, they could introduce their beloved town to America.
FB_IMG_1787324977759 copy.jpg (2639x1280, AR: 2.06)The three trustees — Ed Spoor, Ed Pristov and Lisa Linehan — hit the phones. The volunteer fire department brought lunch-meat sandwiches to the Secret Service. Bob Mramor made bouquets of petunias, lobellias and million bells. Landon Linehan and Connor Reeves welded brackets to hang the flowers on lampposts. Stephanie Siegel promoted the local wine industry. Ruff Neon Signs finally took down the old “ESTAURANT” eyesore. Three to six cops — roughly the same number responsible for all 702 square miles of county land — signed up for off-duty shifts to guard SPIRE around the clock. The trustees watered flowers, picked up trash and enlisted friends and family to help line the road from the interstate exit ramp all the way to campus with about 800 mini American flags.

When SPIRE said it planned to erect a 150-foot-tall flag pole, which was nearly four times the local height limit, the trustees said the academy had to get public approval. “You can’t just ignore the people,” Pristov said. The board of zoning appeals called a special meeting. No one opposed the flag, several attendees said, not even the lifers who always hated change.

The only problem was signs. The turnaround time was too tight for the sign maker, so when people drove into SPIRE, nothing said “Welcome to Harpersfield.” All the press releases, social media posts and ESPN graphics said the Games were happening in Geneva, which has twice as many people and lies 3 miles north.

By showtime, though, the trustees couldn’t have been prouder. They took me on a long tour of the community and praised everyone’s talent and hard work and sacrifice.

“Our community is what makes us so powerful,” Linehan said.

That evening, a crowd roughly the population of Harpersfield showed up at SPIRE. The field house looked like the set of a game show with lights, VIP seats and an obstacle course straight out of “American Ninja Warrior.” The vibe was MAGA rally, with red hats, tributes to Charlie Kirk and one shirt that bore an illustration of Trump and George Washington standing back-to-back and wearing sunglasses. The stands were about three-quarters full.

Helicopter blades thundered outside. The crowd vibrated. The scoreboard showed 45-47. The kids marched in holding state flags and wearing red, white and blue.

* * *

Maybe the only act of defiance of the entire Patriot Games happened when almost the entire fieldhouse was distracted. The president walked out of the tunnel, the announcer screamed “DONALD J. TRUMP!” and the crowd popped.

“We love you!”

“We love you, Mr. President!”

“2028!”

At the top of the bleachers, one kid did not jump to his feet and scream. A boy from the Midwest rose slowly and kept his hands at his sides. He did not clap as Trump led the finalists down a walkway lined by fireworks. He did not clap when they took center stage. He did not clap for the president the entire night. But when the national anthem began, he placed his right hand over his heart.

The crowd was as supportive as the kids had been: They cheered both racers all the way through the finish line and nodded approvingly when the competitors hugged.

For most of the 30-minute competition, Trump did not appear engaged. Even though he sat feet from the course, and even though other VIPs craned their necks to watch the kids race by, Trump sat motionless and kept his eyes on the big screen straight ahead. Once, a girl lost her grip on a gym ring and fell to the ground. The crowd gasped. Trump did not react.
20260812_McGarvey_PatriotGames_2792b.jpg (5088x3392, AR: 1.50)20260812_McGarvey_PatriotGames_1479 copy.jpg (4827x3218, AR: 1.50)20260812_McGarvey_PatriotGames_4572 copy.jpg (5040x3360, AR: 1.50)At halftime, the president did an interview with ESPN. He praised Ohio, listed teams he liked in the upcoming NFL season (the finale of which will be broadcast on ESPN) and lauded the successes of America’s 250th celebrations. “I really am proud of the group of people in this room,” he said. “You see the spirit and the love of our great country. Our country’s never done better.”

Later, Trump helped present the gold trophies. He congratulated the winners, Rockwell Myers from Utah and Kennadi Fuhrman from Kansas, and the confetti cannons boomed. Trump boogied through about half of “YMCA,” and then he waved goodbye and left the stage.

Later, kids would gush on social media, “Best week of my entire life” and “I’m so grateful that I got this opportunity!” They would tell interviewers they’d made new, lifelong friends. One boy would decry “lies on the internet” and say “Freedom 250 did a phenomenal job.”

Marie Paul would say her daughter had new aunties in Hawaii and Alaska. Christian Berezay would keep taking his pills and tinkering with engines. RT Dukes III would post a video in which he tells Trump, “Jesus loves you, Mr. President!”

The township of Harpersfield would go back to debating how to handle SPIRE’s growth, including who would pay for a new stoplight near campus. SPIRE would prepare to start its new school year, and the CEO would say he was only 20% through his developmental master plan.

But that night, after the finals, they went home talking about what a production it all had been. The big American flag twisted in the breeze.

Every kid left with a gold medal just as round and shiny as every other kid’s medal. Everyone said they felt lucky to be a part of something bigger than themselves.

entries.title: Roll Call
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 24, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Time for kids to complain and parents to celebrate. That’s right: D.C. schools are back in session.

Tens of thousands of students are heading back to their classrooms today in D.C.’s traditional public and public charter schools. And for city officials, there’s one goal in mind: to keep as many of those kids there as consistently as possible.

High rates of truancy and absenteeism have dogged D.C.’s schools for years. Last year, roughly 40% of kids were chronically absent, missing 18 or more days of school — whether excused or not. And 35% of students had 10 or more unexcused absences, qualifying them as chronically truant.

Grade level, race and income play a large role in absenteeism and truancy in D.C. According to data from the Office of the State Superintendent of Education, almost 87% of students at Ballou High School in Southeast were chronically absent last year, and 84% were chronically truant. Near the other end of the scale (and city), absenteeism at Janney Elementary School in Northwest stood at 5.1%, and truancy barely exceeded 1%.

But there are signs that things are improving — slowly. A report released this summer by the city’s deputy mayor for education says improvements in getting kids to school are outpacing many other cities. A pilot program implemented last year in a handful of schools with the highest rates of absenteeism and truancy has shown promise: City officials say 71% of truant kids who were engaged in the first year did not become truant in the second. The program is expanding this year, and focusing on ninth- and 10th-grade students — the grade levels where absenteeism and truancy tend to spike.

And there are other efforts to fight truancy. The Richard Wright Public Charter School for Journalism and Media Arts in Ward 6 has focused on keeping kids safe as they walk to school, and will kick the year off this morning with a red-carpet welcome. It’s an effort to “make students feel seen, celebrated and excited about coming to school,” according to Tomeika Bowden, a spokeswoman for the D.C. Public Charter School Board.

D.C. lawmakers will probably continue to focus on how the city can do better in fighting absenteeism and truancy. Ward 5 council member Zachary Parker, for one, has set aside funding for a pilot program in the 2027-28 school year that would pay students $50 a week if they show up. A similar effort in New Orleans showed some promising results.







DEEP DIVE

Order up! It’s Summer Restaurant Week, and more than 200 D.C.-region restaurants are offering diners delicious, discounted dishes to boost business during a slow season.

Wondering where to start? NOTUS food correspondent Tom Sietsema recommends you dine earlier in the week for thinner crowds and speedier service. His choice spots include Ceibo in Adams Morgan, Onggi in Dupont Circle and Del Mar at the Wharf.

If you want the most bang for your buck, a savvy tech wonk created a site that sorts through the city’s offerings for you, Axios D.C. reports. It maps out participating restaurants and points to which have won awards, which are making their Restaurant Week debut and which are “great deals” (with more than 100 listed).

The best deal may be from Brazilian bar Cana, which offers 10 dishes for $65 — a spread that would ordinarily run you $154, City Cast D.C. reports.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Kyle Kirwood AP - 26235742671729 (3332x2222, AR: 1.50)
Another spin? Speaker of the House Mike Johnson and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum both told Fox News that they want to bring the IndyCar race back to the nation’s capital, NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin reports. Outgoing Mayor Muriel Bowser has previously said she hoped the first-ever race would be “followed by second and third.”

“From an economic development for our capital city, hotels, restaurants, the people of Washington, D.C., the greater capital region, all love this idea,” Burgum told Fox. “Everybody I’ve met is saying ‘Please, please do this again next year.’”

American driver Kyle Kirkwood dominated Sunday’s race, setting an IndyCar record for most laps led on a street course, leading for 128 out of 147 laps.

Randy Clarke has entered the chat. Metro’s social-media-savvy general manager jumped into a discussion on X late last week, sharing his thoughts on a post showing that while fare evasion on Metrobuses dropped over the summer, some 63% of riders still don’t pay. Clarke — who has fought to decrease fare evasion on Metrorail, and this year turned his attention to buses — said “it’s not a victimless crime” and addressing it will take more than simply policing.

The Interior Department is prioritizing projects that President Donald Trump thinks will make D.C. “safe and beautiful” while parks projects languish nationwide, The Atlantic reports. Examples include a half-million dollars to replace brick pavers in Lafayette Park, and the $5 million project that included gilding equine statues along the nearby Memorial Bridge.

A second attempt to affix Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center is facing an emergency court challenge, NOTUS’ Torrie Herrington reports. Attorneys for one member of the institution’s board called the move a “breathtaking act of defiance.”





D.C. TRIVIA


Which U.S. president served as chair of D.C.’s first public school board?

  1. Thomas Jefferson
  2. Andrew Jackson
  3. James Madison
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

It’s time for the Commanders to make some hard decisions. Less than a week from today, Washington will have to cut its roster down to 53 players. In the wake of Saturday’s 17-13 preseason loss to the Lions, NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson predicts how those decisions will shape up.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Rockies, 6:45 p.m. (MLB.TV)

entries.title: Johnson’s Gavel Tour
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Speaker Johnson hits the road to keep his job. The Grand Prix could be a yearly D.C. tradition. Political scammers are trying to nab a Trump pardon. The NRCC falls victim to a fraudster. And: A behind-the-scenes look at the Patriot Games.

THE LATEST

On the road again: Speaker Mike Johnson is in the middle of a 30-day campaign stretch stumping for vulnerable House Republicans. But it’s not a selfless effort; he’s also campaigning for his own political future, NOTUS’ Reese Gorman writes from Bethlehem, Pennsylvania.

If Republicans lose the majority in November, the House GOP conference could look for someone else to lead their cause, a possibility Johnson told Reese he isn’t thinking about.

“We're going to win, so I don't have to answer that question,” Johnson said outside a campaign stop for Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in the Lehigh Valley. “I intend to be the speaker going forward.”

Johnson also flipped a joke that Donald Trump makes — that Trump has two jobs, as president and speaker. He said others in the White House view it differently.

“Some on his staff have said, ‘No, it's really like you’re co-president,’” Johnson told NOTUS. “Because the president and I speak all the time.”

It’s Johnson, though, zipping across the country to keep his majority — including by correctly folding and downing a pizza slice with Reps. Mike Lawler and Aaron Bean in New York on Friday — because his political future is up in the air, and names to replace him are already being tossed around. This after a term where his colleagues have openly cursed at and continuously defied him.

As one GOP member put it to Reese, “in the political burn down that’s coming, we slaughter everybody at the front of the room.”

Open tabs: Jeffries and Kushner Meet Privately as Midterm Attacks Fly (NYT); Secret White House bunker undercuts Trump’s ballroom lawsuit, ex-officials say (WaPo); ‘The writing on the wall’: Trump’s staff departs ahead of possible turmoil (Politico); Iran condemns US plans to announce new sanctions (Reuters)

From the White House


Hitting the apex: The summer of America’s 250th celebrations came to a close this weekend with the Freedom 250 Grand Prix IndyCar race, including a special appearance by Trump waiving the green flag after a ceremonial slow spin around the track in the Beast.

Some in Trump’s orbit want to make the Grand Prix an annual event, NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin reports. Speaker Johnson said he’d like “to bring it back next year.” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said there’s “nothing to announce yet” but he’s been inundated with calls for the event to happen again. Even outgoing D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser has said this “first ever” race could be “followed by second and third.”

But Penske is footing most of the multimillion-dollar bill for the event. Company President Bud Denker has said the race “might be the only” Grand Prix D.C. will ever see — and some Washingtonians might be happy about that.

Trump has been granting pardons at record speed this term, and everyone wants in. From granting clemency to the almost 1,600 Jan. 6 rioters to a slew of political allies, the increase in pardon mercy has garnered the attention of a new crop: political scammers. NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause reports today on how three convicted political grifters have asked for the president’s leniency.

The trio collectively swindled tens of thousands of Americans using tactics that included impersonating Trump himself. A White House official told Ben that they had turned down one request and are not actively tracking the others, but the requests show a pardon system that has truly become a free-for-all.

From the campaign trial

The NRCC lost more than $16,300 to an unknown actor, NOTUS’ Dave Levinthal reports, the latest in a litany of thefts that have befallen prominent federal political committees. The NRCC described the “fraud” as from a “foreign country” in an FEC filing but later clarified to Dave that it was unsure the origin of the actor who intercepted a vendor’s payment.

“Protecting donor funds is a top priority for the NRCC,” committee spokesman Will Kiley said. “We caught it immediately, we’re working to recover the funds, and we’ve taken steps to ensure it can’t happen again.”

THE BIG ONE

They loved Jesus, sports and the flag: Every kid left with a medal, as round and shiny as every other kid’s medal, NOTUS’ Sam Fortier reports from the Patriot Games with an inside look at the inaugural competition that earned criticism for its religious overtones and lack of diversity.

The contestants applied through a murky, chaotic selection process, and each was, well, a patriot — a boy and girl from each of the 50 states, plus D.C. and territories. Or sort of. Some kids were representing places they did not live, Sam writes. The girl representing Maine was from New Hampshire; the New Jersey boy went to school in Texas. One boy jokingly cheered on his friend representing Puerto Rico by yelling, “Let’s go Alabama-Virginia-Washington, D.C. — all your states!” On the final day, a seemingly-disengaged Trump flew into the small Ohio town and handed the two winners a check and a gold trophy.

Later, kids would gush on social media, “Best week of my entire life” and “I’m so grateful that I got this opportunity!” They would tell interviewers that they’d made new, lifelong friends. One boy would decry “lies on the internet” and say, “Freedom 250 did a phenomenal job.”

NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

Forget Mar-a-Lago face, writes Elizabeth Evitts Dickinson. The real symbol of right-wing politics is the cinched waist.

NOTUS METRO


Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Sports desk: Who Will Survive the Commanders’ Cuts? Projecting the 53-Man Roster, by Martenzie Johnson

NEW ON NOTUS

An unsettling settlement. The Israeli government moved forward with a plan to build developments in part of the West Bank where Israeli settlements are illegal under international law, NOTUS’ Akbar Shahid Ahmed writes. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) said the plan “purposefully slams the door on the already narrowing prospects for a viable Palestinian state.”

But unlike in previous years, the U.S. is unlikely to stop the move. When asked what the chances were that the Trump administration would block the plans, one U.S. official responded: “Zero.”

More: Democrats Are Getting More Bullish About Taking the Senate, by Igor Bobic

Canada Retaliates Against U.S. Tariffs in Tit-for-Tat Trade War, by Angie Orellana Hernandez

‘Disappointed’: Ranchers and Republicans React to Trump’s Beef Import, by Angie Orellana Hernandez

Rob Bresnahan Blames a ‘Clerical Error’ for a Video a Constituent Alleges Broke House Rules, by Avani Kalra

NOT US

  • Homeland Security Made a Big Claim About Noncitizen Voting. Now It Can’t Prove It. By Nick Corasaniti for The New York Times
  • She’s a Trump acolyte. He’s a ‘gringo Sandinista.’ Meet the Harps. By Terrence McCoy for The Washington Post
  • Russia Tests Readiness for New Round of Military Mobilization, by Thomas Grove and Alexander Ward for The Wall Street Journal
  • Doctors say Trump’s weight poses a significant health risk, by Dan Diamond for The Washington Post

WEEK AHEAD 

Monday 

JD Vance travels to Brewer, Maine, to speak at CompoTech.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent holds a press conference to discuss plans to put economic pressure on Iran.

Tuesday 

Runoffs in the Oklahoma primaries, the South Carolina GOP special primary for Senate and a special election in Georgia’s 13th Congressional District.

Wednesday 

Jeanine John Taele, the man arrested this month at the Trump National Golf Club in Los Angeles, appears in court on a federal weapons charge.

Thursday 

Detention hearing in the case of the Tate brothers, who are facing rape and sex-trafficking charges.

Hearing on an emergency injunction request regarding the planned Trump inscription on the Kennedy Center.

Friday 

Former Fed Chair Jerome Powell speaks at the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium.

Saturday Michigan Democratic Party holds its fall nominating convention in Lansing.

entries.title: Sailor on Nightmare USS Lincoln Deployment Says Border Patrol Arrested His Father
entries.summary: Joshua Aviles described the situation as “heartbreaking.”
entries.content:
A U.S. Navy sailor returning from a record-setting deployment aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln revealed over the weekend that his father was taken into custody by federal immigration authorities while he was serving in President Donald Trump’s ongoing war with Iran.

Joshua Aviles posted an angry message to Facebook about his father’s case, saying he has a driver’s license, social security card and work permit. The son, who had been deployed for over nine months on the beleaguered aircraft carrier, shared that his father was in the process of getting a green card when he was arrested.

“This is heartbreaking for me,” he wrote on Saturday. “I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal. My dad’s only ‘crime’ was coming to this country to give my siblings and me a better life.”

The Department of Homeland Security confirmed Luis Manuel Aviles Roa had been placed in detention. Border Patrol agents took the Nicaraguan national into custody after a traffic stop in Key West, Florida, Saturday, a department spokesperson wrote in a statement.

“Having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws,” the DHS spokesperson wrote. “Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement.”

The USS Lincoln has been deployed for more than 270 days in the war with Iran, but it started heading back to the U.S. last week, following reports of worsening conditions aboard the ship.

The crew of the aircraft carrier spent more than 200 days without a port visit — a record — and the sailors and their family members raised concerns about food shortages, broken toilets and a lack of hygienic supplies that led to the declining mental health of those aboard, according to numerous reports.

Aviles Roa is among the growing number of military parents and spouses who have been detained under the Trump administration. During President Donald Trump’s second term, immigration authorities have taken custody of more than 50 relatives of active-duty military members, according to an investigation by The Associated Press.

entries.title: Michigan Congressional Candidate Says Viral Clip of His Voice Is a ‘Fabrication’
entries.summary: Democratic nominee Jeremy Moss said the audio clip was manipulated and “peddles in offensive tropes and lies.”
entries.content:
Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 11th Congressional District, is facing backlash over a resurfaced audio clip in which he appears to suggest that the primary objective of his campaign is to ensure continued U.S. support for Israel — a clip he now claims is a fake.

“There is a manipulated and unsourced audio, with things I never did and never would say, that is nothing more than political disinformation intended to portray me as anti-American,” Moss wrote last week on X. “It peddles in offensive tropes and lies — especially the lie of dual loyalty suggesting that Jews are never fully citizens of or loyal to their home countries.”

The use of artificial intelligence in campaigns has skyrocketed ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. As the technology becomes more sophisticated — with AI tools able to mimic a person’s likeness, including their voice — it has become harder to tell which video and audio clips are authentic. AI has also crept into some candidates’ political advertising, and federal regulation remains murky on the issue.

It's unclear where the clip of Moss originated and where it was first shared — though it appears to have been online since late last year.

One of his opponents in the Aug. 4 primary, Aisha Farooqi, reposted the clip to X on July 21, and it quickly picked up traction. It was also shared by the American Independence Project, an advocacy group that opposes foreign influence in U.S. elections, on Aug. 7, and received more than 1.5 million views.

https://x.com/AishaforMI/status/2079571368429953509?s=20

Farooqi responded to Moss’ denials by suggesting a forensic analysis could reveal the truth.

“A simple audio analysis can confirm that it is, in fact, your voice and speech patterns,” Farooqi wrote on X last week.

Moss bested Farooqi in the primary by more than 26,000 votes.

The controversy comes as Michigan grapples with growing divisions among its Jewish voters this midterm cycle, with candidates trying to stake out where they stand on Israel. Given Michigan’s status as a battleground state, a few thousand votes can propel a campaign to victory.

In the clip, the voice identified as Moss says, “The entire purpose of my campaign is to make sure America continues to support Israel.”

“I don’t think it’s wrong for Jews in America to want to put Israel first. America is not our homeland and we have been victims of antisemitism here,” the clip continues.

Track AIPAC, a watchdog group that documents financial contributions made by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, posted the video on Reddit on Nov. 24, 2025. The group has also reshared the video since it started going viral in recent weeks.

Farooqi, the American Independence Project and Track AIPAC did not immediately respond to requests for comment Monday.

Moss has been a vocal proponent of Israel’s “right to defend itself” from threats and frequently speaks out against antisemitism, but he has strongly disavowed the content in the clip. However, his post calling it fake garnered little media attention until he spoke with The Detroit News for a story published over the weekend.

Moss told the newspaper that the clip was “either stitched and edited together or just a complete fabrication.” He also said it is part of a “dangerous pattern of things” he’s experienced during his campaign, where U.S. support for Israel has become a flashpoint.

Hasan Piker, a controversial far-left online personality known for his staunch criticism of the Israeli government, spoke about the clip on a recent broadcast, using it to argue that American Jews’ support of Israel was opening them up to violence.

His comment was met with immediate backlash from people in both parties, including Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic nominee for Senate, who campaigned alongside Piker ahead of the primary election. Progressive candidates have faced criticism in recent weeks for appearing on the campaign trail with Piker.

El-Sayed, who has previously spoken out against antisemitism during his campaign, distanced himself from Piker’s comments on Monday.“I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople,” El-Sayed wrote in a statement.

“Hasan Piker's calls for violence against American Jews, and directly naming a Michigan elected official (and future Congressional colleague) Jeremy Moss are unacceptable,” Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Michigan) wrote in a statement Monday. “We should all be calling out this disgusting rhetoric so it loses it’s grip on our politics once and for all. It has no place in Michigan, and no place in our country.”

Moss told Slate he has not yet endorsed El-Sayed because the Democratic Senate nominee is “going to have to demonstrate some serious outreach to Oakland County’s Jewish community.” Moss’ prospective U.S. House district encompasses much of Oakland County, which has the highest population of Jewish voters in the state.

The Michigan state lawmaker is seeking to replace Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who chose to run for Senate instead but lost to El-Sayed in the primary by a small margin.

El-Sayed’s Republican opponent in the general election, former Rep. Mike Rogers, denounced Piker’s comments and called on El-Sayed to do the same. Since winning the Republican nomination, Rogers has been courting Jewish voters in Michigan who might be hesitant to support El-Sayed because of his criticism of Israel.

“Absolutely DISGUSTING,” Rogers wrote on X about the clip of Piker. “If Abdul El-Sayed had any courage at all, he would call this out and disavow Hasan Piker once and for all. We’re waiting, Abdul …”

entries.title: Ace of Trades
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for Aug. 24, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

President Donald Trump threatened to impose even steeper tariffs on Canada this morning after trade talks between the two countries unraveled. All cars and car parts, as well as steel, would be hit with a 50% levy starting Jan. 1 if Trump follows through.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went in front of reporters to outline new economic sanctions on Iran and its trading partners. The measures, called Operation Economic Outcast, include dozens of people and companies, as well as plans to target cryptocurrency and other industries.

  • Iran doesn’t seem concerned, at least outwardly: “The United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries,” Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who serves as speaker of the Iranian Parliament, wrote on social media just before Bessent took the stage.




THE ADMINISTRATION

The Trump administration unveiled a proposal this morning to charge employers who hire workers with H-1B visas a fee of more than $100,000.

  • Déjà vu: Trump tried to implement a nearly identical fee by making a presidential proclamation last year, but a federal judge struck it down earlier this summer.
Federal immigration authorities took the father of a U.S. Navy sailor into custody just as his son was set to return from a record-breaking deployment on the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln.

  • Joshua Aviles posted on Facebook that his father has a driver’s license, social security card, work permit and was in the process of getting a green card when he was arrested.
  • “This is heartbreaking for me,” he wrote.




THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss, the Democrat running to replace Rep. Haley Stevens, claimed that a viral audio recording featuring his voice was faked.

  • Moss said the clip, in which he appeared to state that the primary objective of his campaign was to secure American support for Israel, was “manipulated, either stitched and edited together or just a complete fabrication.” 
  • The clip has reverberated in Michigan politics: Abdul El-Sayed attempted to distance himself from Hasan Piker after the streamer used the clip to suggest American Jews’ support of Israel was opening them to violence.
Mike Rogers' allies have asked AIPAC to shelve its planned advertising on the Michigan Senate candidate’s behalf, Axios reported. Rogers spoke with AIPAC chair Michael Tuchin last week, which led to the pro-Israel group pulling a planned ad attacking El-Sayed.





METRO DESK

An arbitrator overseeing the case of fired Washington Post opinion columnist Karen Attiah ordered the newspaper to rehire her — and shell out back pay to boot. Attiah was let go last year after making several social media posts about the assassination of Charlie Kirk.

  • She said in a statement to The New York Times that she was “willing to go back” to work.

entries.title: Trump Launches Fresh Sanctions Against Iran in Bid to End War
entries.summary: The administration said it’s targeting digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
entries.content:
The Trump administration on Monday broadened its sanctions campaign against Iran and threatened foreign governments and companies with new penalties if they continue doing business with Tehran, as the U.S. seeks to cut off the country from the global economy after months of war.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced sanctions that target digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. The administration also sanctioned more than 60 entities, individuals and vessels it says helped Iran generate oil revenue, obtain nuclear and missile technology and conduct cyber operations.

Bessent said countries and companies are being given individual deadlines to end Iran-related activity identified by the U.S. He would not specify the dates but warned Washington would move quickly against those that do not comply.

He also did not identify the countries that could face secondary sanctions, but China, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates are among Iran’s biggest trading partners.

“Every country has a defined timeline to shut down activities we have identified,” Bessent said at a news conference. “If they do not take action, we will do so unilaterally through Treasury authorities.”

More sanctions are coming, Bessent said, adding that he expects a “major announcement” targeting a financial institution by the end of the week.

The administration is calling the campaign “Operation Economic Outcast,” part of what Bessent has described as an “economic D-Day” against Iran.

But Bessent said Washington is giving governments and companies a chance to change their behavior before imposing the harshest penalties.

“Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent said. “We believe that it is important to level set and give people a cure period, but they should know that that will move very quickly and that we are serious.”

Those that do not comply could lose access to the dollar system, he said.

The administration stopped short Monday of targeting major Chinese banks, which could leave gaps in the U.S. effort to isolate Iran. China continues to buy most of the Iranian oil shipped abroad.

Asked whether Chinese financial institutions could be targeted later, Bessent declined to name potential targets but said no institution was beyond Washington’s reach.

“No one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions,” Bessent said. “If they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted.”

Bessent said Trump is calling foreign leaders directly, with Treasury and State Department officials following up with specific demands and deadlines.

“We know who they are; they know who they are,” Bessent said. “So when the hammer of U.S. Treasury actions falls upon them, they will have no one to blame but themselves.”

The new economic offensive is the latest attempt to end the war, following months of military operations and diplomatic negotiations. The White House initially said it expected the conflict’s military objectives, which began in February, to take four to six weeks.

Trump has repeatedly portrayed Iran as close to defeat even as the war has continued.

“IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!” Trump wrote Monday morning on Truth Social.

Iran is already one of the most heavily sanctioned countries in the world. The administration has spent months tightening restrictions on its oil exports, financial networks and shipping operations. The U.S. blockade of Iranian shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has added another layer of pressure.

That leaves fewer obvious lanes for Washington to apply financial penalties.

Richard Nephew, a former deputy special envoy for Iran who helped design and implement U.S. sanctions policy, said that before Monday’s announcement, most major targets were already covered by existing restrictions.

“The real issue is the implementation side and the degree to which closing off a couple more of these cracks that exist in the sanctions regime is going to materially change things,” said Nephew, who is now at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy. “I think it’s reasonable to be suspicious of.”

Those remaining gaps are mostly enforcement problems, he added, including Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and transactions that continue through foreign banks and companies.

He said the blockade may now matter more than another round of sanctions.

“The blockade is probably doing more of that than sanctions at this point,” Nephew said. “I think sanctions are a secondary issue on this.”

Iranian oil shipments to China fell to roughly 534,000 barrels a day so far in August, down from 823,000 in July, according to shipping data cited by Reuters.

China still buys the vast majority of Iranian oil shipped abroad, according to Kpler. Much of that trade runs through smaller independent refiners rather than major state-owned refiners.

Nephew said that fully isolating Iran would require Washington to confront China more directly, either by threatening Chinese companies with sanctions or offering Beijing something in return for ending its purchases.

“The only way they can do it is one of two things: They either tell the Chinese we’re going to impose sanctions on these companies unless you stop it, or they say, let’s do a trade,” Nephew said.

Washington could go further by targeting major Chinese banks or oil companies. But that would risk retaliation from Beijing.

“There’s a lot we could potentially do, but it’s the blowback question,” Nephew said.

It remains unclear whether more economic pressure can accomplish what months of military action and diplomacy have not: force Tehran into an agreement acceptable to President Donald Trump.

Nephew said the sanctions campaign that preceded the 2015 nuclear agreement produced significant Iranian concessions. He said heavier sanctions imposed since then have failed to produce comparable results.

“You can make a good faith argument, I think, that you are never going to recapture those benefits under a sanctions campaign,” Nephew said.

Bessent on Monday cast Tehran’s coming decision in starker terms.

“Iran now faces a very clear choice, with only two paths before them: complete global isolation and a subsistence economy, or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy,” he said.

Targeting Iranian oil could create problems for Trump at home. Driving more Iranian crude from the market could tighten global supply and push up energy prices as November’s midterm elections approach.

entries.title: Florida Prepares to Roll Back School Vaccine Requirements
entries.summary: A proposed rule represents a step forward in the state surgeon general’s plan to eliminate all vaccine mandates.
entries.content:
Florida is set to roll back four vaccine requirements for children attending the state’s public schools, according to a new rule published Monday by the state Department of Health. The proposed guidelines come after Florida’s surgeon general launched an effort last fall to eliminate all vaccine mandates for school children.

The rule would allow Florida children to attend school without receiving immunizations for chickenpox, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type B and pneumococcal disease. The Department of Health purports that the proposed rule eliminates vaccine mandates for shots that aren’t required under state law.

Florida law requires children to be vaccinated for seven diseases — polio, diphtheria, tetanus, rubeola (measles), rubella, pertussis and mumps — as well as “other communicable diseases as determined by rules of the Department of Health.” The four diseases at issue in the new proposed rule were requirements under the state’s health department, which is now trying to change its own administrative rule.

The period for public comment on the proposed regulation will be open for 21 days.

The push to roll back vaccine requirements in Florida has gained traction under the state’s surgeon general, Joseph Ladapo, who was appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis in 2021.

Lapado has been aligned with other vaccine skeptics and rose to prominence as a member of the group “America’s Frontline Doctors,” which was widely criticized during the COVID-19 pandemic for spreading misinformation about the virus and urging Americans against vaccination.

The group’s founder, Simone Gold, was sentenced to two months in prison for storming the U.S. Capitol building on Jan. 6, 2021. She was pardoned with other Jan. 6 participants by President Donald Trump.

Shortly after assuming his role as Florida’s top medical official, Ladapo reversed COVID-19 quarantine and vaccine requirements. The surgeon general also courted controversy by personally altering data in a study about COVID-19 vaccines to claim that the vaccine posed a higher risk for young men, Politico reported in 2023.

Last year Lapado expanded his efforts to oppose vaccine requirements, saying he plans to eliminate all vaccine mandates for Floridians.

"Every last one of them is wrong and drips with disdain and slavery," Ladapo said about vaccine mandates at a news conference in September.

Measles cases have surged across the country, despite the availability of a vaccine that protects children from the potentially deadly disease and carries relatively little risk of adverse health effects. The Florida Department of Health has reported 155 cases so far in 2026, while just seven cases were reported last year, according to WLRN.

Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Florida), who’s running to replace DeSantis for governor in a race rated “Solid R” by the Cook Political Report, told CBS News over the weekend that he plans to “study” vaccine requirements for polio and measles and committed to working with the state Legislature before making “any of those decisions about requirements for those vaccines.”

Donalds also claimed, without evidence, that the surge in measles cases could be attributed to illegal immigration.

The new wave of vaccine policy reversals in Florida also comes weeks after Trump issued an executive order that would reshape the schedule for childhood vaccines. The president’s policy expanded on earlier efforts by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that were blocked in court.

Trump said the executive order, which made several recommendations such as splitting up certain vaccines into multiple doses, aligned the U.S. “with common sense and knowledge” — though the order was immediately met with criticism from members of the medical community.

The four immunizations at issue in Florida’s new rule were listed as “recommended for all children” in Trump’s executive order.

When asked about Florida’s plan to roll back the requirements last year, Trump told reporters that some vaccines “just pure and simple work” and that those shots “should be used, otherwise some people are going to catch it.”

"I think you have to be very careful when you say that some people don't have to be vaccinated. It's a very ... tough position," Trump said in September.

Lapado has taken a different approach by arguing that bodily autonomy supersedes most public health concerns about vaccines. The state surgeon general called the measles shot “effective” but did not explicitly advocate for Floridians to receive the vaccine at an event in July.
