entries.title: Jake Auchincloss Resigns From Dads Caucus Over Chair Jimmy Gomez’s Ethics Issues
entries.summary: Gomez created the informal group to highlight child care issues, but recent allegations of sexual misconduct triggered a formal ethics investigation.
entries.content:
At least one House Democrat has resigned from the Congressional Dads Caucus, after its chair, California Rep. Jimmy Gomez, became the subject of a sexual misconduct investigation.

Massachusetts Rep. Jake Auchincloss dropped out of the caucus, according to his office. The voluntary congressional group formed for the purpose of advocating to “uplift parents and children across the country,” and is made up of about three dozen Democratic lawmakers, mostly men, according to the caucus website.

“Yes, he has resigned from the Dads Caucus; that leadership is up to the members of the caucus,” spokesperson Georgina Burros responded when asked by NOTUS if Auchincloss planned to call for Gomez to step down as chair.

Auchincloss’ photo has been scrubbed from the caucus website since NOTUS began reporting on this story. It’s not the first time Auchincloss has drawn a line about the personal conduct of a fellow Democrat. He was an early critic of Graham Platner, the former Maine Senate candidate who faced a series of damaging revelations about his past. Auchincloss said that a tattoo of a Nazi symbol Platner got before going into politics was “disqualifying.” Platner eventually dropped out of the Senate race after multiple allegations of sexual misconduct were reported, though he denied those allegations.

The House Ethics Committee announced last week that it was investigating Gomez over sexual misconduct accusations, including an allegation that he engaged in inappropriate sexual conduct with a staffer. The probe followed an April story in the New York Post that alleged Gomez was seen kissing a staffer during the summer of 2023. Gomez subsequently apologized to his wife, family and constituents.

“The Committee notes that the mere fact that it is investigating these allegations, and

publicly disclosing its review, does not itself indicate that any violation has occurred,” the House Ethics Committee said in an Aug. 17 statement. “No other public comment will be made on this matter except in accordance with Committee rules.”

Auchincloss’ resignation from the group is the latest fallout related to the Gomez investigation. A bipartisan group of women called on the House Ethics Committee to rush the release of Gomez’s investigation before the 60-day blackout period ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3. The blackout period restricts certain government communications and ethics investigations ahead of an election.

Gomez founded the Congressional Dads Caucus in January 2023, along with Reps. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, Rob Menendez of New Jersey, Joaquin Castro of Texas, Joe Neguse of Colorado, and former Rep. Jamaal Bowman of New York. During a 2023 House vote to formally elect Kevin McCarthy as speaker that lasted several days, Gomez was seen on the House floor toting his infant son in a baby carrier.

None of the founding members responded to NOTUS when asked if they planned to resign from the caucus or call for Gomez to step down.

When Bowman, who no longer serves in the House, was reached via text for comment about whether Gomez should step down, he responded, “Yes.”

entries.title: Supreme Court Lets Trump Move Forward With Mail-In Voting Rules
entries.summary: The changes could alter how voters can vote by mail in November.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to move forward with parts of the president’s executive order on mail-in voting, ruling Monday that a lower court should not have blocked them.

The unsigned decision wipes out the lower court ruling from Massachusetts that halted, in nearly half of all states and the District of Columbia, two parts of an executive order from March that directed the U.S. Postal Service to create mail ballot rules and the Department of Homeland Security to compile a national database of eligible voters.

The Supreme Court did not decide whether the executive order ultimately is lawful. But the justices set up continued legal clashes over proposed rules to implement the executive order, as states prepare for the midterm elections in November.

Attorneys for the administration had argued in Supreme Court filings that an injunction against the policies was “premature” because the agencies have not yet implemented the executive order, which gave them “substantial discretion” to do so.

The states challenging the executive order contended there would be “extraordinary consequences” if the Trump administration was allowed to overhaul mail-in voting rules so close to the election.

The Supreme Court opinion Monday says that the federal judge should not have blocked a forthcoming DHS rule because states could be harmed by actions the department might take.

“Emphasis on might,” the decision states.

And the opinion says that the USPS is still in the process of proposing a rule that might bind the states in the future.

“Federal courts review final rules, not proposed rules—and certainly not antecedent internal directives to propose a rule,” the opinion states. “If the Postal Service’s final rule harms the States, they may challenge that rule.”

That portion of the opinion states that the USPS rule “is not a proposed rule, let alone a final rule.” But late Friday, the USPS finalized a rule about ballots that would go into effect as early as Wednesday if the Supreme Court allows it.

That highlights a central part of the decision: The Supreme Court emphasized that Monday’s ruling will not be the last action on the implementation of the executive order.

“The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful,” the decision states. “On that score, time will tell.”

A dissent from Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justice Elena Kagan, underscored that point, and contends the states face harms that would allow a judge to step in at this point.

“Today’s decision does not address whether the President’s attempts to interfere with States’ administration of the November 2026 elections are lawful. Nor does it suggest that the Executive Branch has any constitutional or statutory authority to implement the President’s directives,” Sotomayor wrote. “Instead, today’s decision merely postpones adjudication of those challenges.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson also dissented from the decision.

Rick Hasen, a professor at UCLA Law School who focuses on election law, wrote in a blog post that Monday’s decision postpones any kind of ruling on the government’s actions by “a week or two, when we will be even closer to the election and it will be impossible for states to comply with some of the rules that will come out.”

And the Supreme Court decision leaves in place for now another lower court ruling from Massachusetts that blocked the USPS part of the executive order nationwide, in an order that pointed out millions of citizens who rely on mail voting require clarity as to how or whether they will vote in November.

Hasen wrote he expects the lower court judge will now amend that injunction “and issue a new injunction that will stop USPS from implementing its now final rule. And that too may end up at the Supreme Court within a week.”

In the meantime, battleground states are getting set to send out mail ballots soon, including North Carolina on Sept. 4 and Wisconsin on Sept. 17.

Jason Tyson, a spokesperson for North Carolina’s board of elections, said he’d rather not get into hypotheticals about what might happen with the USPS and courts.

“The county boards of elections plan to move forward with sending out absentee ballots to North Carolina voters who have requested them for this election, starting September 4,” Tyson said. “Of course, we will do our best to comply with any court decisions, as we always do.”

entries.title: After a Lackluster Preseason Performance, the Commanders Work Overtime
entries.summary: Coach Dan Quinn said he was bothered by the team’s execution in Saturday’s loss to the Lions.
entries.content:
Dan Quinn insisted that the Commanders’ decision to hold an unscheduled practice Monday was not a knee-jerk reaction to Washington’s 17-13 preseason loss to the Lions on Saturday, but the coach made clear that he was disappointed in his team’s performance.

“I went through a lot of plays, and I didn't feel like we played complementary football,” Quinn said in Ashburn after a full practice that had originally been scheduled as a walkthrough. “That felt in disarray.”

Saturday’s game felt less like a bad matchup and more like a performance that lacked fundamentals and discipline. There were miscommunications on the offensive line, mishaps on the defensive line, and more than twice as many penalty yards (84) as rushing yards (35).

At the postgame press conference, Quinn was short with answers and visibly upset. The team’s walk from the field back to the locker room after the game was solemn and quiet.

At practice on Monday, there were subtle nods to Quinn’s discontent. Coaches yelled for players to run from station to station. Receivers practiced bursting off the line of scrimmage. During two-minute drills, all 11 players on offense would sprint up the field before resetting.

With less than three weeks remaining until the season opener, Washington has plenty of reasons to feel antsy. Pass and run protection, whether from the offensive line, tight ends or running backs, was nearly nonexistent against the Lions. Quinn chalked that up to missed calls, not getting off the ball on time and not holding blocks away from the ball.

The first-team offense ran three total plays and one ended in a sack. The run game mustered 35 yards on 17 carries after totaling 174 yards a week earlier against the Dolphins.

“There were plenty of times I thought, all right, nine [players] are right, these two are wrong, 10 are right, this one’s wrong. So it just didn't feel as connected that I hoped I’d see in the run game,” Quinn said.

But it was in the fundamentals where Washington seemed to struggle the most.

In the first quarter, Lions quarterback Josh Dobbs faked a handoff to running back Jacob Saylors. Rookie linebacker Joshua Josephs went after Saylors, but Dobbs held onto the ball for a 50-yard touchdown run. Quinn said Josephs was supposed to wait out the quarterback’s decision to keep or hand off.

There were two additional plays on third downs where the defender at the end of the line — safety Tyler Owens on one play, linebacker Javontae Jean-Baptiste on another — didn’t contain his area.

“A lot of what I saw, that wasn't us — and that bothered me. And so today is our time to get to the truth,” Quinn said.

Special teams committed four penalties on kickoffs and punts, and on Washington’s final kick return of the day, returner Robert Henry Jr. fumbled the ball back to Detroit.

Most players seemed to understand Quinn’s tone and supported the change to Monday’s practice schedule.

“It’s good,” linebacker Frankie Luvu said. “Just still in camp mode. It’s just work.”

“I don't think we really played to the standard of what we want to do,” rookie center Matt Gulbin said. “So I thought it was good to kind of get moving and have helmets on and have some live action.”

The fiercest response came from safety Jeremy Reaves.

“It's on the schedule, it's time to practice,” Reaves said. “If you got a problem with getting better, this is the wrong job for you. None of us are a complete project. This is the time to do it because Week 1 is too late. So the things that you need to fix, you fix now.”

entries.title: Rep. Al Green Wants to Impeach Trump — Again
entries.summary: The lame-duck lawmaker labeled ICE and CBP as the president’s “paramilitary police forces.”
entries.content:
Democratic Rep. Al Green of Texas is trying to impeach President Donald Trump, even though the lame-duck lawmaker knows he doesn’t have the votes.

Green, who lost his primary runoff in May, cited immigration agents’ fatal shootings of Renee Good, Alex Pretti, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in his 27-page resolution to impeach the president for high crimes and misdemeanors.

“He is abusing the powers of the presidency by operating United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) as his vicious, quota-driven, unaccountable paramilitary police forces, transgressing with anonymity and secrecy, assaulting people, committing and covering up unjustified killings of civilians,” Green’s articles of impeachment state.

Green has attempted to impeach Trump multiple times in both of the president’s terms, including three times last year for what the congressman said was Trump undermining judicial independence, over the war with Iran and for accusing several Democratic lawmakers of behavior the president said was punishable by death.

The White House scoffed at Green’s attempt.

“The brave men and women of ICE and CBP put their lives on the line to arrest murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members, and terrorists,” said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis, “Al Green should be thanking President Trump and our law enforcement for delivering the largest decrease in violent crime in American history.”

The House impeached Trump twice in his first term: in 2019 for withholding military aid for Ukraine and in 2021 after the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. The Senate voted to acquit him both times.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said at a CNBC summit in June that impeaching Trump wasn’t a focus for his party if Democrats take the majority after the midterms.
entries.author: Jackie Llanos

entries.title: The Trump Administration Gives H-1B Visa Fee Another Try
entries.summary: DHS filed a new proposal to charge $103,265 for applications for highly skilled workers.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is again seeking to impose a payment for highly skilled worker visas, this time leaving out visas for educational institutions, nonprofits and governmental research organizations.

The Department of Homeland Security filed a notice Monday outlining its plan to charge a $103,265 fee for H-1B visa petitions. In June, a federal judge stopped the Trump administration from charging $100,000 for workers entering the country under the program, which President Donald Trump said had been abused by technology companies.

DHS is justifying the fee as a way to raise revenue for the costs of administering the legal immigration system. The department estimates it will get $8.8 billion annually and said in the notice submitted to the Federal Register that companies seeking to hire H-1B workers have a greater capability to absorb the cost.

“The scope of the proposed fee increase in this rule is significant,” the notice states. “DHS proposes this cost shifting approach with an emphasis on the ability-to-pay principle for determining user fees. Petitioners for H-1B cap-subject nonimmigrant workers generally are required to have the resources necessary to pay the worker(s) for whom the petition is filed.”

Up to 65,000 H-1B visas are available per year, plus 20,000 for those who have advanced degrees or higher from universities in the country. The fees would apply to everyone applying for those slots, but DHS chose to exempt employees who would be working for higher education institutions and nonprofit and government research organizations.

“Because this is a filing fee, employers would have to pay it with no guarantee that USCIS will approve the petition,” David Bier, director of immigration studies at the libertarian think tank Cato Institute, said in a statement. “Almost no one will risk more than $100,000 with no guarantee of approval.”

DHS’s proposal comes after a federal judge ruled against the fee Trump imposed through a proclamation, labeling the cost a tax that the president didn’t have authority to put in place.

U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin of Massachusetts also found that the fee violated federal statute because the department did not go through the required rulemaking procedures, such as filing a notice, as it did Monday.

“Defendants’ failure to undergo notice-and-comment rulemaking was not [a] harmless error,” Soroking wrote in a June order. “These additional procedures could have altered Defendants’ decision to impose an unconstitutional tax on the H-1B program or, at the very least, required Defendants to consider the impact of the $100,000 payment obligation on regulated entities.”

The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to reinstate the fee last month.

Twenty states sued the administration in December, claiming they would lose vital workers such as teachers, nurses, physicians and researchers as a result of the fee.

The new six-figure fee comes as the administration is weighing charging a similar amount for a work permit that allows international university graduates to work in the U.S. for 12 to 36 months.
entries.author: Jackie Llanos

entries.title: U.S. Removes Syria From State Sponsor of Terrorism List
entries.summary: “These actions represent another historic step by President Trump to give the Syrian people a path to prosperity,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.
entries.content:
The Trump administration has removed Syria from the State Sponsor of Terrorism list, marking a breakthrough for the country, which has carried the label for some 46 years.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio made the announcement formal Monday — 45 days after notifying Congress — to drop the designation for Syria, which is led by Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former terrorist who overthrew the dictatorship of Bashar al-Assad.

Rubio also said the State Department would delist the political and paramilitary group Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham as a specially designated global terrorist. Al-Sharaa led Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham, which helped topple al-Assad's dictatorship in December 2024.

“These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,” Rubio said of the changes. He added that the move would promote Syria’s economic recovery and “reintegration into the global economy.”

Syria was put on the State Sponsor of Terrorism list in 1979. Now, only three countries remain on the U.S. list: Iran, Cuba and North Korea.

In October 2025, the World Bank estimated that Syria's reconstruction would cost $216 billion.

Tom Barrack, the special presidential envoy to Syria, posted on X that removing the state sponsor of terrorism designation is “another decisive step in Syria’s remarkable journey from isolation to partnership.”

“This is not simply the removal of a designation. It is another foundation stone in a new U.S.–Syria relationship built on shared interests, mutual security, and shared prosperity — and another example of @POTUS’s ‘security first, prosperity next’ vision becoming reality,” Barrack posted Monday.

The move had strong bipartisan support in Congress, with Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-New Hampshire), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) and Rep. Joe Wilson (R-South Carolina) — urging Rubio to delist Syria in a July letter.

“Syria’s SST designation represents the most significant remaining legal impediment to Syria’s reconstruction. Its removal could create new opportunity for foreign investment, economic development and capacity building to ensure the Syrians can remain capable and willing partners to the United States,” the lawmakers wrote.

entries.title: Mike Johnson Finds His Midterms Villain in New York: 'Communists'
entries.summary: The speaker’s message focused both on Democrats’ ideology and Republicans’ accomplishments as he campaigned for two Mikes and a Tom in New York and New Jersey.
entries.content:
BETHPAGE, N.Y. — Speaker Mike Johnson crisscrossed New York and New Jersey last week promoting tax cuts from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act while mostly warning voters: Vote Republican to save us from the communists.

House Republican leaders are relying on keeping and flipping a handful of swing seats in and around New York state as their path to holding the majority. But historic trends, President Donald Trump’s declining poll numbers and the rising cost of goods and gas prices aren’t helping.

Now, a crop of democratic socialists who dominated in primaries in New York City districts provide a messaging alternative for Republicans looking to portray every Democrat in the state and nearby suburbs as far-left extremists ahead of the midterms.

“I can be here all day telling you the reasons we’re going to win but ultimately it boils down to one thing: The Democrat Party is being taken over by communists,” Johnson told a room of Long Islanders at the Embassy Diner in Bethpage last week.

Johnson’s economic pitch, delivered mostly to local businesses, was meant to plug tax cuts from the partisan legislation Republicans passed last year. But warnings of communism prevailed from venue to venue. At the Embassy Diner, Johnson delivered them five feet away from a spread of tomahawk steaks, lobster tails, lamb chops and a mountain of shrimp cocktail, some of which were brought out during Johnson’s speech.

The speaker campaigned alongside Mike LiPetri, a former assemblyman working to defeat Democratic Rep. Tom Suozzi in New York’s 3rd Congressional District.
Mike Johson campaigns for Mike LiPetri (3861x2575, AR: 1.50)The district spans parts of Queens, Nassau and Suffolk counties. The median household income is about $140,000 with a per capita income of around $70,000, about 1.5 times the amount in the United States, according U.S. census data. And yet, even some Republican supporters are griping about the cost of living.

“They're way too high,” Anthony Sparaco, 78, a Purple Heart veteran, told NOTUS of gas prices. “You know, we've got to get gas down to the $2 range here — $2 and a little bit of change, maybe.”

Some Republican voters, however, are willing to give the president and their party a pass. MaryAnn Capparelli, 82, from North Massapequa, a “big supporter” of LiPetri’s, said she would like to see political officials talk more about tax cuts, but was hesitant to criticize the president’s decision to go to war against Iran even at the cost of escalating prices.

“I’m all for the president doing what he did. I think the long term would be beneficial for us,” she said, adding, “I just think he's doing his best, and if it takes a little bit longer,” she said before interrupting her own remarks. “I would like to see it end sooner. But I'm for him.”

Trump won the district by 4 percentage points in 2024. That same election, LiPetri lost to Suozzi by just 13,000 votes with little outside help from the party. And even though Trump won’t be at the top of the ticket, LiPetri thinks better name recognition and more fundraising opportunities can close the gap this cycle.

“Now we have a longer runway,” LiPetri told NOTUS. “We’ve raised the money, and more importantly, we show the viability of this race that it can be won so long as we unite.”

Kim Devlin, a campaign spokesperson for Suozzi, told NOTUS in a statement, “MAGA Mike LiPetri and Mike Johnson would simply continue to be rubber stamps in Washington, backing the President’s irresponsible tariffs and reckless war in Iran that are driving up the cost of gas, groceries, and housing.”

New York and New Jersey have become a must-stop for top GOP leaders ahead of November’s midterms.

Trump visited New York twice, campaigning in May for Rep. Mike Lawler of the Hudson Valley and returning this month to support Bruce Blakeman, a long shot opposing New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat. Vice President JD Vance talked to residents on Long Island in June and House Majority Leader Steve Scalise visited the state last week.

Rep. Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey, who faces a serious threat from a Democratic challenger, received a campaign assist from Johnson in Warren County on Friday. It was a rare campaign appearance from Kean following a four-month absence due to mental health issues.

The day before, Johnson visited Silvio’s, a pizza shop in Westchester County, New York, with former baseball player-turned Texas congressional candidate Mark Teixeira and Rep. Aaron Bean of Florida to campaign with Lawler.

Separately, Johnson was the special guest at a LiPetri fundraising event in Upper Brookville with Frank DellaFera of Fera Pharmaceuticals, a specialty drug company focused on eye health, according to its LinkedIn page. Tickets ranged from $500 to $25,000. Johnson mentioned at his stop at the diner that the fundraiser hosted by a GOP challenger was “record breaking.”
Mike Johson campaigns for Mike LiPetri (3861x2575, AR: 1.50)Unlike LiPetri’s run two years ago, the two-time candidate and other Republicans in the tri-state area have become the recipients of extraordinary financial backing from Republicans — especially the financial arms of the party. The Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with the speaker, has reserved $18.6 million for the New York City media market. LiPetri received an early financial boost as part of the National Republican Campaign Committee’s MAGA Majority program, which ensures early support for candidates in competitive seats. He was added to the program in March — six months earlier than his last run at the seat.

“Two-Faced Tom Suozzi has left Long Islanders behind for too long,” NRCC spokesperson Maureen O'Toole told NOTUS in a statement. “Instead of fighting for them, he’s put his own interests first by voting against increasing the SALT cap, siding with Democrat extremists like Kathy Hochul and Zohran Mamdani, and lining his pockets trading stocks. Long Islanders are ready for change, and Trump-backed Mike LiPetri will get the job done in November.”

Democrats aren’t holding back either, almost ensuring New York will be home to some of the most expensive races this cycle.

“HMP is all in on defeating Mike Lawler and Tom Kean Jr., and will do whatever it takes to defend seats like NY-03 blue on our way to taking back the House in November,” House Majority PAC spokesperson CJ Warnke said in a statement.

The increase in the state and local tax deduction cap that was included in the 2025 Republican tax bill could become a bright spot for otherwise disaffected voters. Sparaco said legislation that raised the deduction to $40,000 from $10,000 “helped tremendously.”

“I guess with those savings, I'm able to afford a little higher prices in gas and food and everything else,” he said.

But those tax cuts expire in 2029, and it’s not clear Republicans will have the support for an extension.

“There are extensions and deadlines on some of these cuts, and so that's why you have to elect new people to come in to reinforce the troops and make sure that they continue to fight for the state's interests,” Johnson told reporters when pressed on whether he’d support extending the tax breaks.

But that would require Republicans to maintain their majority. And for all Johnson’s messaging about communism, he’s mindful of another factor: turnout.

“In 2024 — think of this — 10 races that decided the majority in the Congress was decided by 6,000 votes,” Johnson told the audience. “Every single vote counts — especially in New York.”
